title: Random Sampling
intro: Recognize and justify random sampling methods, specify an implementable selection process, and distinguish strata from clusters.

moments.title: With and without replacement
moments.text: Replacement determines whether a unit can be selected again.

moments.title: Simple random sample
moments.text: Every possible sample of the specified size has equal probability.

moments.title: Why equal individual chances are insufficient
moments.text: An SRS requires equal chances for entire samples.

moments.title: Implement random selection
moments.text: Label units, generate random labels, and state the stopping rule.

moments.title: Stratified random sampling
moments.text: Take a random sample within every stratum.

moments.title: Choose useful strata
moments.text: A stratifying characteristic should relate to the outcome.

moments.title: Justify the choice
moments.text: Match the design to the population, question, and practical constraints.

moments.title: Cluster sampling
moments.text: Select clusters randomly and observe all units in selected clusters.

moments.title: Systematic sampling
moments.text: Use a random start and a fixed interval.

cards.name: SRS
cards.text: Every group of the target size has the same chance of selection.

cards.name: Stratified
cards.text: Divide by a relevant characteristic, then sample some units from every stratum.

cards.name: Cluster
cards.text: Randomly select some clusters, then observe every unit within those clusters.

cards.name: Systematic
cards.text: Choose a random starting position, then take every kth unit.

cards.name: Replacement
cards.text: Specify whether repeats are possible; without replacement, select distinct units.

questions.obj: Describe an implementable simple random sample
questions.q: The video wants an SRS of 40 students from Valley City High School. Explain a process using the school's complete enrollment list.

steps.t: Assign distinct labels to all eligible students.

work.text: Number every student on the complete list once, using equal-length labels if using a random-digit table.

steps.t: Select labels with a random mechanism.

work.text: Use a generator that selects labels uniformly. For sampling without replacement, ignore repeated labels and any labels outside the list.

steps.t: State when selection stops and who is included.

work.text: Stop after 40 distinct valid labels and include the corresponding students.

questions.answer: This procedure makes every set of 40 students equally likely, assuming the list is complete and the generator is fair.

questions.q: The video proposes sampling students by grade level, taking a random sample of 10 freshmen, 10 sophomores, 10 juniors, and 10 seniors. Identify and justify the design.

work.text: Each grade is a nonoverlapping stratum.

steps.t: Identify the random selection within groups.

work.text: Take an SRS of 10 students from each grade and combine the selected students.

steps.t: Connect the grouping to the question.

work.text: If opinions differ by grade, this guarantees each grade is represented and can improve precision compared with an unstratified sample.

questions.answer: This is stratified random sampling, not cluster sampling: some students are selected from every grade.

traps.title: Equal individual chances
traps.weak: Equal chances for each person prove an SRS.
traps.better: Every possible sample of the requested size must have equal probability.

traps.title: Strata versus clusters
traps.weak: Sampling everyone from two selected classes is stratified.
traps.better: It is cluster sampling when classes are randomly selected and everyone in those classes is included.

traps.title: Systematic start
traps.weak: Take every tenth person, starting with the first.
traps.better: Choose the start randomly among the first ten positions, then take every tenth person.

traps.title: Guaranteed representation
traps.weak: Random sampling guarantees the sample matches the population.
traps.better: Random sampling reduces selection bias, but chance imbalances remain possible.

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: The video occasionally describes systematic sampling as using a random interval. The design uses a fixed periodic interval after a random start. Stratifying guarantees inclusion from the chosen strata, not perfect representation on every characteristic.

questions.stem: An office samples 12 employees randomly from each department. What method is used?
why: Some employees are selected randomly from every department.
Cluster sampling would select departments and include everyone in them.
Chance selection within departments is specified.

questions.stem: A city randomly selects five blocks and interviews every household on those blocks. What is the design?
why: Households are selected together by blocks, so not every household sample is possible.
It does not sample some households from every block.
Blocks are randomly selected and all their households are included.
Households are selected by the design, not an open invitation.

questions.stem: Choose a start uniformly from 1 through 20, then select every twentieth record. This is:
why: Only a subset of records is selected.
There is a random start and fixed interval.
Many possible groups of records cannot be selected.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest reason to stratify a student opinion survey by grade?
opts: Opinions may differ by grade and every grade should be represented
why: Variation remains within and between samples.
Random selection is used within strata.
A sampling design does not force opinions to agree.
Relevant strata ensure coverage of groups and may improve precision.

sections.title: Write a complete response
sections.prompt: A college has a complete list of 2,400 students, including 600 in each of four years. It wants a sample of 120 students to study access to course advising.
parts: (a) Describe an SRS of 120 without replacement.
(b) Describe a stratified random alternative by year and justify it.
(c) A proposal instead selects three mixed-year tutorial groups randomly and surveys all their students. Identify the method and one possible advantage.
sample: (a) Label students 0001 through 2400. Select labels uniformly at random, ignoring repeats, until 120 distinct valid labels are obtained. Survey those students.
(b) Take an SRS of 30 students within each year using the four complete year lists, then combine them. Access to advising may differ by year; stratifying ensures every year is represented.

(c) This is cluster sampling. It may be easier to contact students together in selected tutorial groups, reducing collection costs. Mixed-year groups may resemble the wider population, although representativeness is not guaranteed.
checklist: Uses the complete list and unique labels.
Specifies uniform chance selection, no repeats, and a stopping rule.
Justifies strata in the context of advising.
Identifies clustering and a practical advantage.
